strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem (single-image demoiréing) and correctly identifies the difficulty of disentangling texture corruption from color distortions in direct image-to-image restoration.
Quantitative results are strong on FHDMi (25.26 PSNR / 0.8518 SSIM / 0.1253 LPIPS) with clear margins over strong baselines (ESDNet-L, FHDê²Net, MBCNN), and competitive results on UHDM.

The efficiency angle is a genuine contribution: 6.065M parameters and 2.49 TFLOPs for 4K, substantially smaller than MopNet (58.6M), MoCE-IR (11.5M), and comparable to ESDNet-L while outperforming it, which is valuable for high-resolution/edge deployment.

The ablation study is reasonably thorough, covering crop-vs-resize training, learnable FCT, per-branch behavior (Table 5), hierarchical fusion/RDDB (Table 6), and a decomposition comparison (Table 3/4).
The frequency visualization in Fig. 2 (2D/3D RGB curves for high/low components of moiré vs. clean images) provides useful intuition supporting the design.
The paper is well organized and clearly written, with an informative pipeline figure and sensible two-stage training strategy.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in the core 'frequency decomposition.' With the stated kernel (Eq. 1, a normalized Gaussian-like 3x3) and the recursion (Eq. 2), the formulation collapses to I_h = I_m - I_l and I_l = lowpass(I_m) (i.e., a blurred image), since I_h^0 = 0 makes I_h^i = I_m - I_l^i at every level. This is essentially a Gaussian/Laplacian-pyramid high-pass/low-pass split rather than a fundamentally new decomposition, and the claim of a 'novel frequency decomposition' is overstated.

The Haar-wavelet ablation (PSNR 13.32, SSIM 0.2113) is implausibly poor and directly contradicts prior successful wavelet-based demoiréing works (WDNet, AWUDN, MBWDN). This strongly suggests an implementation/training issue in that ablation rather than a fundamental inferiority of the Haar transform, so the conclusion drawn from it is not reliable.

Several components are combinations of existing ideas (channel attention + gated FFN + RDDB) presented with somewhat inflated novelty language; the SA-CA module in particular is an assembly of prior blocks.
The 'state-of-the-art' framing is inconsistent with the UHDM table, where Freqformer is second in PSNR (22.22) behind ESDNet-L (22.42); the claim should be qualified.
Relevant wavelet-based demoiréing methods discussed in Related Work (AWUDN, MBWDN) are not quantitatively compared in the main tables, weakening the empirical positioning of the method.

The task framing is muddied by attributing low-frequency color distortions partly to moiré and partly to dataset construction/color shifts; it is unclear how much of the reported gain comes from correcting dataset color shifts versus genuine moiré removal.
The abstract advertises publicly available code but the URL is blank, and there is no limitations or broader societal-impact discussion, which weakens reproducibility and completeness.

strengths: Strong and consistent empirical results: Freqformer achieves state-of-the-art performance on both FHDMi (PSNR 25.26, SSIM 0.8518, LPIPS 0.1253) and UHDM (PSNR 22.22, SSIM 0.8018, LPIPS 0.2434), outperforming or matching much larger baselines, and remains competitive against recent general-purpose restoration models (AdairR, MoCE-IR, OSEDiff) that have up to ~1B parameters.
Good efficiency/performance trade-off: only 6.065M parameters and 2.49 TFLOPs for 4K inference, which is a meaningful practical contribution for deployment on high-resolution and edge devices.

The core motivation is well-supported by evidence: the frequency-decomposition visualization (Fig. 2) clearly shows that moiré textures are concentrated in high-frequency components while color distortions dominate the low-frequency component, and this analysis directly drives the dual-branch design.

Comprehensive ablation study (Tables 3-6) covers the low-branch resize strategy, learnable FCT, two-branch vs end-to-end training, per-branch performance, and the hierarchical fusion / RDDB design choices, which strengthens the credibility of the individual design decisions.
The paper is clearly organized and written, with a coherent pipeline figure and clear formulation of the decomposition, the learnable Frequency Composition Transform, and the SA-CA module.

The insight that the low-frequency component is scale-robust (allowing aggressive resize) while high-frequency content is spatially local (allowing random cropping) is practically valuable and leads to a clean and reusable training strategy.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: frequency decomposition for demoiréing (WDNet, AWUDN, MBWDN) and dual-branch frequency-aware architectures are already established. The main novelties are a different fixed low-pass kernel, a learnable fusion module, and an attention block that largely recombines existing components (RDDB, channel/spatial attention, gated FFN). The paper does not clearly articulate what is fundamentally new relative to this prior work.

The comparison against the Haar wavelet transform is suspicious and may be an unfair/strawman baseline. Reporting PSNR 13.32 and SSIM 0.2113 for the Haar-based model is implausibly poor for a functioning model; this suggests either an implementation issue or an inconsistent training setup, so the claim that the proposed decomposition is inherently superior to wavelet decomposition is not convincingly established.

The proposed decomposition kernel (Eq. 1) is a fixed hand-crafted low-pass filter and is essentially a special case of a smoothing operator; the paper does not justify why this particular kernel is preferable to other (e.g., learned or Gaussian) low-pass operators, nor is it ablated.

The claim that the low-frequency branch is robust to scale (reconstruction PSNR ~50 dB) is based on a single internal measurement with limited detail; the scaling factor, data, and evaluation protocol are not fully specified, weakening this supporting evidence.

The SA-CA module is a combination of known components, and while the ablation in Table 6 shows it helps, the gains from hierarchical fusion (0.8786 -> 0.8782 SSIM, essentially flat) and from RDDB are marginal; the significance of these components is not clearly established.
No discussion of limitations, failure cases, or societal impact; the abstract states that code is publicly available but no URL is provided in the manuscript, which weakens reproducibility claims.

Several baselines in Table 1 are shown with N/A for some metrics, and it is not stated whether comparisons were run under a unified protocol (e.g., same training data, same crop/resize at inference), which could affect the fairness of the SOTA claim.

strengths: Strong and consistent quantitative results: Frequformer attains the best PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on FHDMi (25.26 / 0.8518 / 0.1253) and best SSIM/LPIPS on UHDM (0.8018 / 0.2434), clearly outperforming ESDNet-L, FHDε²Net, MBCNN and MopNet on the primary benchmark.
Efficiency is well supported: 6.065M parameters and 2.49 TFLOPs for 4K inference, competitive with or smaller than ESDNet-L, AdaIR, and MoCE-IR, matching the paper's compact-model claim.

The paper is generally well organized and readable, with a clear problem statement and a useful frequency-domain analysis (Fig. 2) motivating the separation of high-frequency texture and low-frequency color distortions.

A reasonably thorough ablation suite (Tables 3–6) isolates resize-vs-crop training, the learnable FCT, hierarchical fusion, and RDDB, and the two-stage training schedule is described concretely enough to follow.
The related-work section is well organized and correctly positions the method against image, video, and raw-domain demoiréing literature, and against wavelet-based approaches.
Comparing against general image restoration models (OSEDiff, AdaIR, MoCE-IR) as well as demoiréing-specific methods is a sensible and informative choice.
weaknesses: The claimed 'novel frequency decomposition' is essentially a fixed-kernel Gaussian/Laplacian pyramid: a fixed 3×3 averaging kernel with dilation 2^i followed by I_h = I^{i-1} - I^i is a standard multi-scale blur-subtraction scheme, and the decomposition itself is not learned. The novelty claim is therefore overstated, and the text itself says the design is 'inspired by [37],' a super-resolution paper, further undercutting the originality claim.

The learnable Frequency Composition Transform (FCT) is presented as a contribution but the paper itself states that the addition of the two branch outputs 'is mathematically equivalent to F = Conv(Concat(...))', i.e., a single convolution on concatenated features plus a transformer block. This is a minor implementation detail rather than a substantive architectural idea, and the 'doubles the number of bias parameters' justification is unconvincing.

The Haar-wavelet ablation (Sec. 4.2) reports PSNR 13.32, SSIM 0.2113, LPIPS 0.7574 — an implausibly catastrophic result, since a 2-level Haar transform with a correct inverse should be near-lossless and any network built on it should land in a normal range. This strongly suggests an implementation bug rather than a fundamental limitation of wavelets, yet this experiment is the primary evidence that the proposed decomposition beats existing wavelet-based demoiréing. The central claim therefore rests on a suspect comparison.

Claims are not well calibrated to the evidence: the abstract states 'state-of-the-art performance,' but on UHDM the method is second in PSNR (22.22 vs. ESDNet-L's 22.42), and 'significantly outperforms' overstates a 0.38 dB PSNR gain on FHDMi.

Architectural novelty is limited: SA-CA is standard channel attention plus a gated FFN, RDDB and hierarchical fusion are borrowed from prior work (with citations), and the dual-branch frequency design closely mirrors existing wavelet-based dual-branch networks (WDNet, MBWDN). It is not made clear what the paper advances beyond careful engineering.

Reproducibility and completeness are uneven: the code URL in the abstract is left blank, no runtime/latency measurements are given despite the strong efficiency claims, and no variance or error bars are reported for any metric.
The paper includes no limitations discussion and no societal-impact/broader-impact statement, which weakens the overall scientific framing of the contribution.

strengths: The core motivation is well supported empirically: the paper visualizes (Fig. 2) that moiré texture is concentrated in high-frequency components while color distortion dominates the low-frequency component, and derives a dual-branch design with an asymmetric training scheme (crop for high-frequency, resize for low-frequency). This is a sensible, non-arbitrary design choice rather than a generic two-stream network.

Strong empirical results across four benchmarks: Freqformer ranks first on TIP2018, LCDMoire and FHDMi on PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, and best on SSIM/LPIPS with near-best PSNR on UHDM, while using only 6.065M parameters and 2.46 TFLOPs. The accuracy/efficiency trade-off relative to MopNet (58.6M), MBCNN (14.2M) and ESDNet-L (10.6M) is a genuine practical advantage for 4K demoiréing.

The ablation suite is reasonably thorough and informative: decomposition vs. 2-level Haar DWT and Block DCT (Table 3), crop vs. resize vs. crop&tile for the low-frequency branch (Table 4), learnable vs. fixed FCT and with/without frequency decomposition (Table 5), and component ablations on hierarchical fusion, RDDB, SCP and DAT (Table 6).

The resize-based low-frequency training insight is a transferable finding: the authors verify with a controlled experiment (≈25 dB reconstruction for the high-frequency component vs. ≈50 dB for the low-frequency component under resize) that the low-frequency component can be safely downsampled, and they reproduce the benefit on ESDNet-L (Table 4), which strengthens the generality of the claim beyond their own architecture.

The critique of existing frequency tools is clearly articulated (shift variance of Haar, block artifacts/local-stationarity assumption of DCT, channel fragmentation/redundancy, error accumulation with fixed inverse transforms), and the learnable Frequency Composition Transform is a reasonable answer to the fixed-inverse-transform problem.
The paper is generally well organized and readable, with informative figures (Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 6, Fig. 7) and a clear statement of training protocol and hyper-parameters.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty relative to the framing. The proposed 'novel frequency decomposition' is essentially a Laplacian/Gaussian-pyramid-style decomposition (fixed 3x3 blur, residual I_h = I_l^0 - I_l^i) plus a learnable fusion; the dual-branch architecture, channel attention, gated FFN, and hierarchical fusion are standard components. The novelty claim in the abstract/introduction should be moderated to reflect that the contribution is primarily an effective system design and empirical study.

Technical soundness of the decomposition in Eqs. (1)-(3) is questionable and underspecified. Convolving a fixed 3x3 Gaussian-like kernel with dilation rate 2^i is a sparse (comb-sampled) filter, not a proper low-pass filter; it can pass aliased high-frequency content, which contradicts the paper's claims of 'anti-aliasing' and 'smoothness-preserving'. The paper never states the number of decomposition levels L used, its sensitivity, or whether an explicit downsample/blur is performed. A precise definition of the operator plus an aliasing analysis (or frequency response plot) is needed.

Fairness/clarity of the main comparison is insufficient. The ESDNet row in Table 1 reports FHDMi PSNR 22.12, which is considerably below values reported in the original ESDNet paper; the manuscript does not state whether the Table 1/Table 2 baselines were retrained or re-evaluated under the same protocol, resolution, and crop size as Freqformer, nor which numbers are quoted from prior work. Since the central claim is state-of-the-art performance, this must be made explicit and, where possible, verified under a unified protocol.

The SOTA claim is slightly overstated for UHDM: Freqformer is second in PSNR (22.24 vs. 22.42 for ESDNet-L) and the abstract/introduction phrase 'state-of-the-art performance' should be qualified per dataset and metric.

The ablation tables are ambiguous and potentially misleading as presented. Tables 4 and 6 report 29-30 dB PSNR for branch-level models, far above the full-model 25.26 dB on FHDMi. It is never stated that these are evaluated on the decomposed components (rather than the full clean image), so the tables cannot be interpreted without guessing the evaluation target; the target and metric definition must be stated in the captions.

The design justification for the learnable FCT is weak: the paper notes that separate convolutions followed by addition are mathematically equivalent to a convolution on the concatenated features (differing only in bias parameters), which does not by itself explain why the proposed formulation is preferable to the simpler equivalent. A clearer motivation (or an ablation isolating the PostFusion transformer block) would help.

Missing contextualization and analysis: there is no comparison against recent (2023-2025) demoiréing models beyond those listed (e.g., MoiréDet, P-BiC, and diffusion-based demoiréing), no failure-case analysis, and no discussion of limitations or broader impact. The slower 4K inference (0.58 s vs. 0.25 s for ESDNet-L despite fewer FLOPs) is acknowledged only in passing, and the practical consequence for the claimed edge-device deployment is not examined.

Some reproducibility details are incomplete: the two-stage training schedule (epochs per stage, learning-rate schedule interactions, loss weights for the joint stage), the exact composition of PostFusion, and the treatment of the interpolated low-frequency features/crops during joint training are described only briefly, and the code is only promised.

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: the paper clearly articulates why direct image-to-image demoiréing struggles and why frequency separation is a promising direction, supported by an insightful 3D/2D RGB visualization (Fig. 2) showing moiré textures concentrate in high frequencies while color distortions concentrate in low frequencies.

The asymmetric dual-branch training strategy (crop-based for the high-frequency/texture branch, resize-based for the low-frequency/color branch) is a genuinely interesting and well-justified design. The ablation in Table 4 convincingly shows that resize-based training for the low branch substantially outperforms crop/crop-tile variants, including on ESDNet-L, demonstrating the insight generalizes.

Thorough and well-organized ablation studies covering the frequency decomposition (vs. Haar DWT and Block DCT, Table 3), the learnable FCT (Table 5), the low-branch resize strategy (Table 4), and architectural components including RDDB, SCP, hierarchical fusion, and the SA-CA vs. DAT block (Table 6). This is more than most comparable papers provide.

Strong quantitative results across four benchmarks (TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, UHDM), with consistent gains in PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, and the model is compact (6.065M parameters) relative to strong baselines such as MBCNN (14.19M) and MopNet (58.57M).
Useful qualitative analysis (Figs. 6 and 7) showing both moiré and color-distortion removal, which supports the central claim that separating texture and color handling is beneficial.
The paper is generally well-written and the pipeline figure (Fig. 4) and method description are reasonably clear.
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty. The frequency decomposition kernel in Eq. 1 is a fixed, hand-crafted Gaussian-like kernel explicitly taken from Wang et al. [33], and the recursive dilated convolution is a heuristic construction rather than a learned or fundamentally new decomposition. The SA-CA module is essentially a standard channel-attention + gated FFN block similar to CBAM/Restormer/DAT, and the dual-branch architecture with attention is common in this literature. The claim of a 'novel frequency decomposition' in the contributions list overstates the novelty.

Overstated claims relative to results. The abstract and contributions claim 'state-of-the-art performance,' but on the hardest benchmark (UHDM) the method is second in PSNR (22.24 vs. 22.42 for ESDNet-L) and only marginally ahead in SSIM/LPIPS (Table 1). The framing should more carefully acknowledge this rather than asserting blanket SOTA.

Efficiency claims are partially misleading. The paper emphasizes compactness and suitability for edge deployment, yet Freqformer has higher FLOPs (2.46T vs. 2.24T) and is more than twice as slow at 4K inference (0.58 s vs. 0.25 s) than ESDNet-L. The slower runtime is only briefly acknowledged and the 'efficient' framing is not fully consistent with the latency evidence.

Limited direct evidence for some design claims. The statement that low-frequency reconstruction PSNR is ~50 dB is used to justify aggressive downsampling, but the exact protocol (which images, which scale, how measured) is not reported. Similarly, the 'dataset-related color shifts' argument is asserted rather than analyzed.

Comparison scope is somewhat narrow in Table 1: several recent demoiréing methods (e.g., recent transformer-based or diffusion-based demoiréing works) are absent, so the SOTA claim is only established against a subset of the literature. The generative baseline comparison (Table 2) is informative but the interpretation of one-step diffusion results is not fully developed.

The paper does not include a dedicated limitations section or broader societal-impact discussion, and failure cases / out-of-distribution robustness (e.g., on real captured moiré at arbitrary scales) are not discussed.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and challenging low-level vision problem (single-image demoiréing) with an intuitive motivation: moiré artifacts can be disentangled into high-frequency texture corruption and low-frequency color distortion.

The dual-branch asymmetric training scheme (crop-based for high-frequency, resize-based for low-frequency) is well motivated by the empirical observation that low-frequency components are highly scale-robust, and is supported by a dedicated ablation (Table 4).

The experimental section is reasonably extensive, covering four benchmarks (TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, UHDM) with quantitative metrics, visual comparisons, and several ablation studies; implementation details (optimizer, schedule, loss weights, resolutions) are reported.
The model is compact (~6M parameters) and achieves competitive/leading PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on several datasets, suggesting a favorable accuracy-to-size trade-off.
Related work is well surveyed, covering CNN-based, wavelet/DCT-based, Raw-domain, and video demoiréing methods.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the proposed 'novel frequency decomposition' is essentially a fixed Gaussian-like low-pass filter. Since the kernel k is not learned and Eq. 3 reduces to I_h^L = I_m − I_l^L, the recursive formulation collapses to a simple high-pass residual, making the 'L-level recursive decomposition' largely redundant.

The 'learnable' Frequency Composition Transform (FCT) is essentially concatenation followed by a convolution and a transformer block; the authors themselves note it is mathematically equivalent to Conv(Concat(...)), so it is a minor engineering choice rather than a principled contribution.

The SA-CA module combines existing components (channel attention in the style of Restormer, RDDB from RDN, gated FFN) and is not clearly differentiated from prior art, weakening the claimed architectural contribution.

The frequency-decomposition ablation (Table 3) is not controlled: the Haar-DWT and Block-DCT variants change both the transform and the network architecture/parameter count (10.9M and 12.7M vs 6.065M), so it does not isolate the effect of the decomposition itself.

Experimental numbers are inconsistent across tables: FHDMi PSNR is reported as 25.26 in Table 1 but 29.20 for 'Freqformer (High branch)' in Table 6, with no explanation of the discrepancy or of what the high-branch-only setting measures.
Anomalous metric behavior on UHDM (a ~0.09 SSIM and LPIPS gain over ESDNet-L despite a lower PSNR, 22.24 vs 22.42) is unexplained and raises concerns about evaluation consistency or metric alignment.

Efficiency claims are undermined by the reported latency: 0.58 s/image at 4K versus 0.25 s/image for ESDNet-L, despite fewer FLOPs; the repeated claims of suitability for 'edge devices' and 'high-resolution inference' are therefore not well supported.
Novelty is overstated in the abstract and contributions ('novel frequency decomposition,' 'state-of-the-art'), which does not match the incremental nature of the components.
Code is not released ('will be made publicly available'), which limits reproducibility given the several non-trivial design and training choices.
